causes.text: At the American Heart Association meeting on November 18 2024, Eli Lilly reported that its experimental pill muvalaplin lowered lipoprotein(a) levels by 70 % to nearly 86 % in a mid-stage trial. With no approved treatments for elevated Lp(a), the results highlighted the commercial potential of the first oral therapy targeting this genetic cardiovascular risk factor.

source_info.title: Lilly pill cuts genetic form of cholesterol nearly 86 % in study

effects.text: Merck entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals on March 25 2025 for HRS-5346, an investigational oral small-molecule inhibitor of lipoprotein(a), agreeing to pay $200 million upfront and up to $1.77 billion in milestone payments. The deal granted Merck worldwide rights outside Greater China to develop and commercialize the therapy, expanding its cardiovascular pipeline.

source_info.title: Merck enters exclusive license agreement for HRS-5346

causal_reasoning_chain.description: Eli Lilly's November 2024 presentation showed that its oral pill muvalaplin could reduce lipoprotein(a) levels by up to 86 % in a mid-stage trial. As there are no approved therapies for elevated Lp(a), the data suggested that an effective oral inhibitor could unlock a lucrative new market in cardiometabolic disease.

Industry commentators predicted that Lilly's success would attract significant investment and that the first companies to market would enjoy substantial competitive advantage. Merck, which lacked an Lp(a) program, recognized the risk of being left behind and began evaluating external candidates.

On March 25 2025, Merck announced that it had licensed HRS-5346 from Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals for a $200 million upfront payment with potential milestones totaling $1.77 billion. Investors welcomed the move as a timely response to Lilly's progress; Merck's shares edged up about 0.5 % as the company positioned itself to compete in the emerging Lp(a) market.

rationale: Lilly's strong muvalaplin data highlighted the potential of Lp(a) inhibitors and threatened to give the company a head start in a new therapeutic area.  To avoid missing out, Merck quickly secured rights to HRS-5346, signalling to investors that it would contend for leadership in the nascent market.
counterfactual_analysis: If Lilly's trial had been less impressive or if other competitors had not demonstrated strong results, Merck might not have prioritised an Lp(a) program.  Without a clear competitive impetus, the company may have deferred investing billions of dollars in licensing an early-stage cardiovascular drug.

adversarial_confounders.text: Amgen's olpasiran and Novartis' pelacarsen, both injectable Lp(a) inhibitors under development, also showed promising data and may have influenced Merck's strategy.
adversarial_confounders.impact: Multiple competing programs could have collectively motivated Merck to license HRS-5346, independent of Lilly's results.

details.commentary: Lilly's promising Lp(a) pill data signalled that a new class of cardiovascular drugs could emerge, potentially limiting Merck's future share of this genetically defined market. By licensing HRS-5346, Merck moved to ensure it had its own contender in a field that might otherwise be dominated by early movers.

details.pestel_factor: Technological - Innovation in cardiometabolic drug modalities
details.commentary: Breakthroughs in cardiovascular genetics and trial design are reshaping treatment guidelines, with regulators and clinicians looking for ways to address risks like elevated Lp(a) that previously had no therapies. These technological and medical trends made it logical for Merck to invest heavily in a similar oral mechanism, hoping to capture demand that emerges as awareness and screening grow.

Positive mid stage data in a new mechanism attracts capital and research attention, which accelerates development and increases the chances that the mechanism becomes a standard of care. Merck's deal builds on this reinforcing loop by expanding the pool of companies pursuing Lp(a) targets, further entrenching the idea that this pathway deserves significant investment.
